name: Adam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions or AI firms. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, a junior lineworker at the electricity company. I take the evening fault rota for extra pay, check the truck with Priya and help restore damaged lines; I like the moment the lights return, but she's still teaching me difficult terminations.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is on your mind when you leave work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ellis teaches at our children's primary school, and we have a mortgage. We've saved about ten months of expenses, which gives us room to breathe, but I still want to be good enough at this trade to earn my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster form is fine if the company keeps paying for people who know the line. My pay is good because I take the evening fault rota, not because I'm the best climber on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still slow on awkward terminations and ask for a check before we energise. But we have about ten months' expenses saved, my partner has a wage, and several utilities hire nearby, so a quiet AI year doesn't threaten the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on the evening fault rota and book one extra supervised termination with my lead each month. I'll keep the company's paper isolation checklist in my pocket when the office changes a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to concentrate on the trade. I don't love new screens, but I'm more bothered by making a mistake on a real line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you enjoy about the evening rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a storm trips a feeder, you can watch a row of houses come back one by one. I like being useful, even if my lead Priya still has to correct my hand placement sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is home like after one of those shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ellis teaches at a primary school, and our two children are still there too. We have a mortgage, but the ten-month fund means I can sleep after a short run of bad shifts.

say: I'd say **faster forms** are fine while the company still values trained lineworkers.
I would explain my higher pay comes from the **evening fault rota**, not senior skill.
think: My **awkward terminations** still need supervision, even when routine software changes little.
Ten months' savings, Ellis's wage and **nearby utilities** make this mild scenario manageable.
do: Stay on the **evening fault rota** and book an extra supervised termination monthly.
Carry the **paper isolation checklist** when office forms change.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and focused on avoiding a physical mistake.
S0.quote: My pay is good because I take the evening fault rota, not because I'm the best climber on the truck.
fieldNote: His high wage reflects **shift allowance**, while he freely admits needing correction on difficult physical work.
A **ten-month fund** and Ellis's school wage make ordinary job uncertainty less immediate for this household.

steps.text: Stay on evening fault rota and book monthly supervised terminations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying and scheduling software might save office time, but the crew needs the right cable and a safe plan. I'd bring that up at the union meeting rather than argue with a screen on the roadside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The field work changes slower, yet a leaner office could push rushed plans onto apprentices and juniors. I don't use AI tools and wouldn't be first to volunteer, though I could learn a proved system if Priya showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'll take two mistaken material orders to our union safety meeting and ask for a field sign-off before jobs are released. I'll keep taking evening faults; if my hours drop for a quarter, I'll apply at the two neighbouring utilities I've worked alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about more pressure on a junior crew. I'm not frightened of losing the mortgage next month, because our savings buy time to look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with a material order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work ticket showed a lighter cable than the one on the pole. My lead Priya stopped us at the yard, and the office corrected the cable ticket before we drove out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a new planning tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the crew has checked it on real jobs and Priya can show me the steps. I'm slow with new screens, and I won't pretend I know a fault code I haven't learned.

say: I'd raise **material accuracy** and field sign-off at our union safety meeting.
I would tell colleagues the **crew must check** a software plan before going to the site.
think: A leaner office may pass **rushed plans** to juniors while the physical repair still needs people.
Our savings and **nearby vacancies** buy me time if hours fall, though I dislike new screens.
do: Bring **two wrong orders** to the union safety meeting next week.
Keep taking **evening faults** and apply to two neighbouring utilities if hours fall for a quarter.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but our fund keeps a short spell of reduced work from becoming a crisis.
S1.quote: My lead Priya stopped us at the yard, and the office corrected the cable ticket before we drove out.
fieldNote: He treats a real **wrong-cable incident** as a collective safety concern and plans to raise it through his union.
He is **slow to adopt software**, yet accepts a tool once the crew has tested it on actual jobs.

steps.text: Bring two mistaken material orders to union safety meeting
Continue evening fault shifts while available
Apply to two neighbouring utilities if hours fall for a quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that thinking AI by 2028 could remove planners first, while line crews still work with their hands. Around 2031 the robot reaches our side of the gate, and we need a bargain about jobs and safety before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when full thinking AI arrives and 48 when the robot can do my physical work. Ten months saved is a real buffer, but every nearby utility could buy the same machines; I can't count on a vacancy forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the union steward to put retraining wages and human safety sign-off on the bargaining agenda. In 2029 I'll keep working the line, finish my supervised fault sign-offs and apply for a paid substation apprenticeship if the utility advertises places; I know robots might reach substations too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed about a trade disappearing faster than a contract can be rewritten. The fund keeps me from panicking, but it doesn't tell me what work pays after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a substation apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped on a few substation callouts, so it isn't a leap into work I know nothing about. I'd still need instruction, and I wouldn't spend our mortgage fund on unpaid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the steward for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written wage while people train, a rule naming who signs off an isolation, and notice before any junior positions are cut. I'd ask for those at the next branch meeting, not wait until a robot is on a truck.

say: I'd tell the union **2028 AGI** hits planning first, while 2031 robots could take physical linework.
I would press for a **jobs and safety bargain** before robots arrive.
think: At 48, even **nearby utilities** may have fewer vacancies if all buy capable robots.
Our **ten-month fund** gives time to act, but cannot replace a whole trade's wages.
do: Put **training wages** and safety sign-off on the union bargaining agenda now.
Keep line shifts and **fault sign-offs** in 2029, then apply for paid substation training if offered.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, although savings give me enough room to make a plan.
S2.quote: Ten months saved is a real buffer, but every nearby utility could buy the same machines; I can't count on a vacancy forever.
fieldNote: He sees the difference between **temporary savings** and a durable job when all regional employers may automate.
His plan combines **union bargaining** with continuing paid work and a conditional apprenticeship, without assuming substations are safe.

steps.text: Ask union steward to bargain for paid training and human isolation sign-off
Continue line shifts and finish supervised fault sign-offs in 2029
Apply for paid substation apprenticeship if places are advertised in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives our union time to ask the company for numbers, not slogans. Thinking work changes by 2031 and the robots reach linework around 2034, so both dates belong in the contract talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 at the second. Our children would be older and savings could still help, but I don't assume school costs end cleanly or that I can retire at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll stand for the safety committee seat and ask the company how many field posts it expects through 2034. By 2032 I'll apply for a paid substation training slot if the agreement protects my wage, and until then I'll keep taking fault calls with Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier with five years, but I can feel the clock. A committee seat doesn't repair a line, yet it might force an answer before families have to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stand for the seat yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was the junior who carried the wrong cable ticket, and I can describe how a bad order reaches a truck. I don't need to be the best climber to ask a clear safety question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the company gives no numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to record the refusal and bargain for notice and paid placements anyway. I'd also check neighbouring utilities' vacancies, though robots may change those too.

say: I'd demand **field-post numbers** for 2034 before our union signs a new agreement.
I would put **both AI dates** into contract talks because planning and climbing change at different times.
think: At 51, I cannot assume **retirement** or the end of children's costs solves lost line wages.
My savings help, but **regional automation** could limit even the nearby jobs I normally count on.
do: Stand for the **safety committee** this year and ask for field-post forecasts.
Apply for **paid substation training** by 2032 if wages are protected, while continuing fault calls.
feel: I feel **steadier but pressed** to get an answer before families must guess.
S3.quote: I don't need to be the best climber to ask a clear safety question.
fieldNote: He turns a **junior mistake** into a reason to represent workers on the safety committee.
The extra years let him demand **workforce numbers** and a paid route, while recognising regional jobs could also shrink.

steps.text: Stand for union safety committee and request field-post forecasts
Apply for paid substation training if wages protected by 2032
Continue fault calls with Priya while training terms are negotiated

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to put a proper training right into the agreement, not just a promise on a poster. Thinking AI arrives by 2036; line robots around 2039 are the date that matters most to my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 and then 56. We might have paid much of the mortgage by then, and our children will be grown or close, but I can't assume pension income or a safe line job at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking supervised complex faults now and ask our union to negotiate paid training time at the next contract round. By 2037 I'll apply for a utility-funded substation course if it has posted jobs, and Ellis and I will keep the ten-month fund intact rather than spend it on a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more patient than in the short version. I still don't like the idea of handing in my badge before I choose to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already have ten months saved, and the children and house still need money now. I would keep the fund where we can reach it, but I wouldn't call that putting more away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the union cannot win training time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for posted utility work while it exists and ask for public training support that pays a living wage. I wouldn't tell another junior to fund a long private course on hope.

say: I'd push for a **paid training right** in our next union agreement.
I would tell the crew **2039 robots** threaten linework after thinking AI changes the office in 2036.
think: At 56, I cannot assume **pension income** or a permanent line job.
Older children and a smaller mortgage may help, but **family costs** will not vanish automatically.
do: Keep taking **supervised complex faults** while wages continue.
Ask the union for **paid training time** and apply for posted substation work by 2037 if funded.
feel: I feel **patient but sad** at the thought of leaving linework before choosing to stop.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell another junior to fund a long private course on hope.
fieldNote: His ten-month fund remains **existing savings**, not a new saving action or a substitute for wages.
The long warning lets him seek **contract rights** and conditional paid training, while still expecting physical automation.

steps.text: Continue supervised complex fault calls on the line
Ask union to bargain for paid training time next contract round
Apply for utility-funded substation course if jobs posted by 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the union has so little time to secure paid paths before robots reach the line. Written training wages, notice before junior cuts and a named person responsible for safety checks would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets blamed for a dangerous plan made by software. I'd want a field worker to be able to stop a job without losing pay when the plan and the pole don't match.

headlineQuote: I'd want a field worker to be able to stop a job without losing pay when the plan and the pole don't match.
portrait: Adam is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** whose evening fault allowance lifts his pay above the usual rate.
Ellis's teaching wage, **ten months saved** and several nearby utilities give the family room around its mortgage and school costs.
He avoids unfamiliar software and values **union safety bargaining**, while admitting his difficult terminations still need supervision.
Fast AGI and robots **alarm** him; longer warnings allow a committee role and conditional paid substation training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to negotiate paid alternatives before field robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written training wages**, notice before junior cuts and named responsibility for safety checks would let him plan.
